content: Malabsorption of fat and protein is a significant issue in individuals with cystic fibrosis, contributing to poor nutritional status. This condition is often exacerbated by impaired pancreatic function, which can lead to increased gastric acidity. Elevated gastric acidity may result in symptoms such as heartburn and peptic ulcers, and it can also interfere with the effectiveness of oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. To address these issues, gastric acid-reducing agents have been used as an adjunct to pancreatic enzyme therapy, with the aim of improving fat absorption and alleviating gastrointestinal symptoms in people with cystic fibrosis. However, it is critical to evaluate the evidence supporting the potential benefits of these drugs in this population. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of gastric acid-reducing drug therapies on various outcomes, including nutritional status, symptoms related to increased gastric acidity, fat absorption, lung function, quality of life, and survival. Additionally, the review sought to determine whether these therapies are associated with any adverse effects. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic and non-electronic database searches, as well as handsearches of journals, abstract books, and conference proceedings. The most recent search of this register was performed on April 26, 2021. On the same date, further searches were conducted on the clinicaltrials.gov registry to identify ongoing trials. The WHO ICTRP database was last searched in 2020 but was unavailable for further searches due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The review included all randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared agents reducing gastric acidity to either placebo or other comparator treatments. Both authors independently selected the trials, assessed their quality, and extracted the relevant data. A total of 40 trials were identified, of which 17 trials involving 273 participants met the inclusion criteria. However, the number of trials evaluating each specific agent was small. Seven of these trials were conducted exclusively in children, while four were limited to adults. The trials were all single-center studies, with durations ranging from five days to six months. Fourteen of the trials employed a cross-over design, but insufficient information was available to perform comprehensive meta-analyses. The reporting quality of the included trials was generally inadequate, making it difficult to assess the risk of bias. One trial demonstrated that gastric acid-reducing therapies improved gastrointestinal symptoms, such as abdominal pain. Seven trials reported significant improvements in measures of fat malabsorption. However, two trials found no significant improvement in nutritional status. Only one trial assessed respiratory function, and another reported an adverse effect associated with the prostaglandin E2 analogue misoprostol. No trials evaluated the impact of these therapies on quality of life, complications related to increased gastric acidity, or survival. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence suggesting that gastric acid-reducing agents may improve gastrointestinal symptoms and fat absorption in individuals with cystic fibrosis. However, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether these therapies improve nutritional status, lung function, quality of life, or survival. Furthermore, due to the unclear risk of bias in the included trials, definitive conclusions cannot be drawn from the available evidence. The authors recommend conducting large, multicenter, randomized controlled trials to better evaluate the efficacy and safety of these interventions.
